questions.question: Trace the implications of agricultural revolution on the social life of early humans.
questions.solution_html:
• / - The agricultural revolution forced humans to abandon their million-year-old
  • foraging lifestyle and settle permanently near fields - leading to the emergence of
  • permanent farming villages like Jericho by 8,500 BCE - The shift to cereal-based diets
  • proved nutritionally damaging, as such diets were poor in minerals and vitamins, hard
  • to digest, bad for teeth, and created dangerous dependence on single staples
  • vulnerable to bad weather or insect attacks - Dependence on land made early
  • agricultural communities targets of conquest and violent attacks, with fifteen percent
  • of total deaths and twenty-five percent of male deaths in agricultural societies caused
  • by violence - Women began giving birth every year, causing exponential population
  • growth, though child mortality rose alarmingly to one in every three births, reflecting
  • the harsher living conditions of settled life - The need to protect surplus food
  • production compelled early humans to build walls, guard cereal stores and fields, and
  • invent new tools like hoes, plows, and stone grinding instruments, fundamentally
  • transforming their material culture - Humans also began domesticating animals
  • through selective breeding, castration, and careful species selection, progressively
  • making animals fatter and more submissive while using them for food, raw materials
  • and muscle power, fundamentally reshaping huma n relationships with the natural
  • world.
questions.final_answer: world.

questions.question: Discuss various theoretical approach towards the study of violence.
questions.solution_html:
• Historical Sociology: Weber and Elias linked declining violence to state intervention
  • but twentieth-century state-sponsored atrocities and regional variations undermined
  • this thesis - Psychology: Freud attributed violence to repressed biological aggression
  • Foucault critiqued modernity as inherently violent, and crowd theorists identified
  • irrational destructive tendencies in collective behaviour - Anthropology: Gluckman
  • and Davis challenged Eurocentric civilizing narratives, redefining violence as culturally
  • embedded and empha sizing negotiated justice over state coercion - Evolutionary
  • Psychology: Pinker linked declining violence to biological self -control, but critics
  • argued violence derives from social relations and honour codes rather than biological
  • determinism - Interdisciplinary Studies: The most comprehensive approach integrates
  • social relations, state -civil society dynamics, emotional factors, environmental
  • destabilizers, and political enmity, rejecting linear deterministic frameworks.
questions.final_answer: destabilizers, and political enmity, rejecting linear deterministic frameworks.
